summary:
Remember the last index of every code in a hash map. When a code appears again, check whether its previous
index is at most `k` back. Only the most recent occurrence matters, since it's the closest. O(n) expected.
Sorting `(code, index)` pairs and checking neighbours is an O(n log n) alternative.

question.md:
Return whether some code appears twice at positions `i < j` with `j − i ≤ k`.

- **n up to 10⁵**, codes from −10⁹ to 10⁹, `k` up to 10⁵.

think.md:
`codes = [5, 1, 8, 2, 1, 9, 8, 3]`, `k = 2` → **false** (the 1s are 3 apart, the 8s 4 apart). With `k = 3`
the answer would be true.

Looking back from position `j`, only the window of the previous `k` codes matters, and only whether `codes[j]`
is in it. The closest earlier copy is the last one, so a last-position map answers that in O(1).

approaches.title: Compare with the next k codes

idea.md: For each `i`, look at `i+1 .. i+k` for an equal code.

lines.text: Any equal code within the next `k` positions.

complexity.md: **Time O(n · k):** 10¹⁰ comparisons at the limits. **Space O(1).**

steps.text: Code 5 at 0: no repeat within reach.
Code 1 at 1: no repeat within reach.
Code 8 at 2: no repeat within reach.
Code 2 at 3: no repeat within reach.
Code 1 at 4: no repeat within reach.
Code 9 at 5: no repeat within reach.
Code 8 at 6: no repeat within reach.
Code 3 at 7: no repeat within reach.
Answer: false.

walk.title: For each code, compare it with the next k = 2 codes.

limits.md: Each code is compared with up to `k` others. Remembering where each code was last seen makes it one lookup.

idea.md: Sort indices by `(code, index)`. Equal codes end up adjacent and in increasing index order; check each adjacent pair with equal code for a gap ≤ `k`.

lines.text: Order positions by code, then by position.

notes.java: Pack code and position into one long (positions fit in 20 bits) and sort primitives.
notes.c: Sort (code, position) pairs stored side by side.

lines.text: Between equal codes, the closest pair is adjacent in this order.

steps.text: Code 1 at 1 and 4: 3 apart, more than 2.
Code 8 at 2 and 6: 4 apart, more than 2.
Answer: false.

walk.title: Sort (code, position) pairs. Equal codes become neighbours, ordered by position, so only neighbouring pairs need checking.

limits.md: Sorting costs O(n log n); a hash map of last positions answers each check in O(1) expected time.

approaches.title: Last position of each code

idea.md: Scan left to right with a map `last[code] = index`. If `code` was seen and `i − last[code] ≤ k`, return true; then update `last[code] = i`.

build: Map from code to last index.

notes.c: A small open-addressing hash table: at least twice as many slots as codes, so probes stay short.
Hash the code and probe forward to its slot (or an empty one).

lines.text: The previous copy is the closest one; within `k` means yes.

notes.java: `put` returns the previous index, if any.

lines.text: This position is now the last one.

complexity.md: **Time O(n)** expected. **Space O(n)** (a window set of the last `k` codes would be O(k)).

steps.text: Code 5 at 0: first time.
Code 1 at 1: first time.
Code 8 at 2: first time.
Code 2 at 3: first time.
Code 1 at 4: last seen at 1, 3 back.
Code 9 at 5: first time.
Code 8 at 6: last seen at 2, 4 back.
Code 3 at 7: first time.
No gap was ≤ 2: false.

walk.title: Remember the last position of every code. A code is a repeat within reach if its last position is at most k back.

takeaways.md:
- **"Duplicate within distance k":** last-index map, or a set of the last `k` items.
- Only the most recent occurrence matters.
- Sorting pairs is the no-hashing fallback.
